newsitem.title: USA: IBM has e-mail problems on Internet service.
newsitem.headline: IBM has e-mail problems on Internet service.

text.p: International Business Machines Corp confirmed that it is having problems with electronic mail on its Internet access service, ironically a day after PC World rated IBM's as one of the best Internet access services.
Late Wednesday, CNET, an Internet-based technology news service, reported that an unspecified number of users of IBM's Internet service are having delays receiving e-mail.

An IBM spokeswoman confirmed that it has had some problems delivering electronic mail to users of its Internet access service, which is called the IBM Internet Connection. But she said that IBM has had "no reports of significant mail loss."

IBM also said that as part of its policy, it does not deliver mail to users in excess of two megabits in size, so that it does not exceed the capacity of a user's mailbox. The spokeswoman said she did not have any numbers on the amount of users affected by the problems in mail delivery.

"We have been aware that there have been slowdowns," the spokeswoman said, adding that the problems were "sporadic" and were likely triggered after IBM switched to a flat-rate pricing plan of $19.95 a month last July. IBM does not disclose how many users it has of its little-known service.
She said IBM is in the process of upgrading its network.

IBM is working on adding new software code to the servers that store and dispatch electronic mail to subscribers, it has doubled its disk capacity on the servers and it is upgrading all of its servers to increase capacity by four times.

In its February issue, which hit newsstands Tuesday, PC World gave IBM glowing reviews. PC World said that IBM's Internet access service was the winner in a survey of 12 leading Internet service providers, where its service was rated A-plus in the survey of 3,800 online users.
"This kind of stuff can happen to any ISP," said Brad Grimes, senior associate editor at PC World.

"We haven't gotten any complaints...and in IBM's case, we did not have any e-mail lost," Grimes said, adding that PC World staffers ran their own tests of e-mail over all the Internet access providers surveyed over a two week period.

Analysts said that IBM is not alone with e-mail problems over the increasingly congested Internet. Last November, half of the 425,000 users of AT&T Corp's WorldNet service were hit by a problem in AT&T's servers that halted e-mail delivery, which was later restored.
"It's another day in life on the 'Net," said Ted Julian, an analyst with International Data Corp.
"The unfortunate thing is that portions of the Net go down," Julian said. "This will become a way that network providers are differentiated, is how robust their networks are."
IBM's Internet access service was first introduced in October 1994, as part of its OS/2 Warp operating system. I is now available for Windows-based PCs and Apple Computer's Macs.
Arlen Communications, a market research firm in Bethesda, Md., estimates that users of IBM's Internet Connection number in the "low thousands."
